title: Histories of Tacitus
subtitle: the Roman historian's account of the civil wars after Nero
lead: The Histories is a Latin history by Cornelius Tacitus. He says at the start that he begins with the year Servius Galba was consul for the second time (1:1), and that the age he is entering on was "rich in disasters, terrible in its battles, torn by revolts, and savage even in peace", with four emperors dead by the sword and three civil wars (1:2). The five books that survive tell the year AD 69, when Galba, Otho and Vitellius were each emperor for a few months and Vespasian, whom the armies of the East made emperor, won the throne. Book 5 takes up Titus in Judea and the origin of the Jews (5:1-2) and breaks off in the middle of a sentence at 5:26.

It is not Scripture for anyone. It is a Roman senator's history, and it is on this site for context. It shows the world of the Roman emperors in which the New Testament was written, and it gives a Roman's account of Judea: the Jews' origins and customs (5:2-13), Pompey, Herod, the governor Felix, and the army that went up to Jerusalem. Book 4 tells how Vespasian healed two men at Alexandria (4:81-84), a story to set beside the Gospels' healings. The notes mark every place where the Histories names a person, place or event that the Bible or Josephus also names, and say how sure the match is.
facts: Historiae, "the Histories" (the title of the Perseus Latin text)
Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman senator (consul in 97), born about AD 56
Written about AD 100-110 (Wikipedia); the LacusCurtius introduction says between 104 and 109. It tells the years from AD 69, a generation or more earlier.
Narrative history of the Roman Empire after the death of Nero

Books 1 to 4 and the first 26 sections of Book 5. The LacusCurtius introduction says the Histories were written in fourteen books, so most of the work is lost, including Tacitus's account of the fall of Jerusalem.
The surviving text rests on one manuscript, the Second Medicean (Laurentianus 68, 2), copied in the eleventh century at Monte Cassino (LacusCurtius introduction).

Five books survive, 389 numbered sections in all (90, 101, 86, 86 and 26). On this site each of Tacitus's books is one chapter and each numbered section is one verse. The text ends in the middle of a sentence at 5:26.

The Conversational English Translation, a free modern rendering made from the Church and Brodribb English (1864), with that English and the Latin of C. D. Fisher's Oxford Classical Text (1911) offered beside it. Both come from the Perseus Digital Library under CC BY-SA 4.0.
authorship: The Perseus texts give the author as Cornelius Tacitus. At 1:1 he speaks in the first person and says that Galba, Otho and Vitellius did him "no favors and no harm", and that Vespasian started his career, Titus raised it and Domitian took it further. Wikipedia gives his career as quaestor in 81 or 82, praetor in 88, suffect consul in 97 and proconsul of Asia in 112-113, and says he married the daughter of the general Agricola in 77 or 78. It says he was born in 56 or 57 in a province that is not known, and that he died about 120, no earlier than 116 (a passage in the Annals fixes that date). The LacusCurtius introduction puts his birth about 55-56 and says that what we know of his life comes chiefly from his own works.

Wikipedia dates the work about 100-110 and says that, complete, it covered AD 69 to 96. The LacusCurtius introduction says Tacitus was at work on it between 104 and 109. The work itself dates its writing from its first section: Tacitus calls Nerva "divine" and Trajan the ruler, and says that if he lives long enough he has saved their reigns for his old age (1:1). The title "divine" is the Senate's honor to an emperor after his death (see the note at 1:15), so Nerva was dead and Trajan was reigning when Tacitus wrote that.

Tacitus names few of them. He gives Vipstanus Messalla, a tribune in the Flavian army, as his authority (3:9, 3:25, 3:28) and says that, on whether Hormus (as Messalla tells it) or Antonius (as Gaius Plinius tells it) thought of pointing the troops at Cremona, he cannot easily decide between them (3:28, haud facile discreverim). He names Cluvius Rufus and Silius Italicus as the two who heard the talk between Sabinus and Vitellius (3:65). Wikipedia lists Cluvius Rufus, Fabius Rusticus and Pliny the Elder among the authorities he cites in his works, and official records such as the Senate's minutes. In Book 4 he gives the Alexandria healings as still told by those who were present (4:81) and the story of the god Serapis as the Egyptian priests tell it (4:83). In Book 5 he says "most writers agree" and names none (5:3); Josephus names Manetho and Lysimachus for the same leper-exile story (Against Apion 1.14-35).
Pliny the Younger was a friend of Tacitus. Wikipedia says Pliny's two letters on the eruption of Vesuvius were sent at Tacitus's request.

Tacitus also wrote the Annals, which cover the years before the Histories. The Histories cite two passages of it that matter for the Bible's world: the governor Felix as the brother of Pallas (Annals 12.54) and Nero's punishment of the Christians (Annals 15.44, quoted in the notes at 5:9).

audience.to: Romans of the early second century. Wikipedia's page on the Histories dates the work to about AD 100-110 and says Pliny the Younger wrote to Tacitus of "your histories"; Nerva was dead and Trajan reigned when Tacitus wrote (1:1). Tacitus counts the 820 years since Rome was founded and the writers who told "the story of the Roman people" (1:1). He calls Pompey "the first Roman to conquer the Jews" (5:9), and "our" is Roman throughout. He explains what a Roman reader might not know, such as the temple of Venus at Paphos (2:2), the god Serapis, whose origin "hasn't yet been made well known by Roman writers" (4:83), and the Jews (5:2-13), and he does not explain legions, consuls, procurators or Roman Knights, which his readers knew. Beyond that, the texts we have opened name no reader. The Wikipedia page on the Histories says Tacitus was sure that only the emperor could keep peace, the armies' loyalty and the empire together.
audience.why: At 1:1 he says that after Actium, when peace made it necessary for all power to go to one man, "those great minds disappeared" and truth suffered, through ignorance of public affairs, flattery or hatred of the rulers. He says that anyone who promises untouched honesty "has to speak of every man without affection and without hatred", and he admits his debt to the Flavian emperors. At 1:4 he says he will review the city, the armies, the provinces and the strengths and sicknesses of the whole world so that readers understand "not only the turns and outcomes of events, which are mostly chance, but also the reason and causes behind them". At 1:1 he also says he has saved the reigns of Nerva and Trajan, a time when "you can think what you like and say what you think", for his old age; so he wrote about AD 69 after Domitian's death, with the freedom of that time. Wikipedia says he and his property survived Domitian's reign of terror (81-96), but the experience left him "jaded and perhaps ashamed at his own complicity," with a hatred of tyranny evident in his works. For the Jews' chapter (5:2-13), Bloch's study, reviewed by Pieter van der Horst, finds that Tacitus follows his predecessors on the Jews in general, that even features he does not present negatively "receive a non-positive colouring," and that the impression he aims at is that the Jews fully deserved to be defeated and to have their only temple destroyed.

outline: Galba, Otho and the Rhine armies (Tacitus's Book 1, 1 January to 14 March AD 69). Why Tacitus writes, the disasters of the age, and his verdict on the gods
Rome, the armies and the provinces when Nero died, including the war in Judea (1:10) and Tiberius Alexander in Egypt (1:11)
Galba adopts Piso (10 January); Otho is made emperor (15 January); Galba, Vinius and Piso are killed in the Forum; the Senate goes to Otho
Rome fears both men; the Rhine legions hail Vitellius and send two armies toward Italy; letters between the rivals; a night riot, omens and a flood; Otho leaves Rome on 14 March

The Year of Four Emperors: Bedriacum, Otho and the Rise of Vespasian (Book 2). Titus turns back from the road to Rome; the temple of Venus at Paphos; Vespasian, Mucianus and an East that waits; a false Nero
Otho's armies and Vitellius's armies in northern Italy; the battle at Bedriacum; Otho's last words and death
Vitellius's army wins; reprisals, feasting and the riot at Ticinum; a false Scribonianus Camerinus
Vespasian weighs the risks; Mucianus's speech; omens (the cypress, Carmel); Vespasian is hailed at Alexandria and by the army of Judea; the East lines up and the Illyrian legions rise
Vitellius moves on Rome; first news of revolt; Caecina and Bassus turn

Book 3: Cremona, the Capitol and the Fall of Vitellius. The Flavian leaders argue; Antonius invades Italy; Caecina's treason; the night battle outside Cremona; the assault on the camp and the sack of Cremona
Vitellius in Rome; Fabius Valens flees and dies; the provinces choose Vespasian; the Flavian army crosses the Apennines; Vitellius gives up the throne in the Forum
Sabinus takes the Capitol; the Capitol burns (3:71-72); Domitian escapes; the battle for Rome; Vitellius is found and killed; Domitian is hailed as Caesar

After the Victory: Rome, the Rhine and Alexandria (Book 4). Rome after the victory: the Senate honors Vespasian, Helvidius Priscus and Marcellus quarrel, the first informer is tried, Mucianus takes control
The revolt of Civilis begins on the Rhine: the Batavians, the Canninefates, the Old Camp besieged, Hordeonius Flaccus murdered
Rome: the Senate meets on 1 January; Domitian in the Senate; Regulus on trial; the Praetorian Guard; Vespasian, Titus and Domitian; the Capitol is rebuilt (4:53)
Gaul thinks Rome is finished: the plot of Classicus, Tutor and Sabinus; the Old Camp falls; Cerialis arrives and breaks the revolt
Vespasian at Alexandria: the healings (4:81-82) and how the god Serapis came to the city (4:83-84)
Domitian is held back at Lugdunum
The Road to Jerusalem, and Civilis on the Rhine (Book 5). Titus marches on Jerusalem

The Jews: five stories of their origin (5:2); Moyses and the flight from Egypt (5:3); customs and the reasons given for them (5:4-5); the land, the Jordan and the Dead Sea (5:6-7); Jerusalem, its temple and its rulers (5:8); Rome and Judea from Pompey to Felix (5:9); the war comes back to Jerusalem and the three commanders (5:10-12); signs from heaven and the start of the siege (5:13)
Civilis and Cerialis at the Old Camp: the battle in the marsh, the dam, the night raid, Cerialis offers terms, Civilis asks to talk. The text breaks off in the middle of his speech at 5:26

lenses.name: Christian reading
lenses.desc: How a Christian who takes the Bible as true reads the passage, and where the Bible's own account of the same years, people and places stands beside it. The site's own voice.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Historians and classicists: what Tacitus knew and where he got it, how his account compares with other writers, and how scholars judge him, each with named holders.

lenses.name: Roman world
lenses.desc: What the first readers knew: the emperors and their courts, the legions and provinces, Roman religion, law, offices and customs.

lenses.name: Jewish and early Christian writings
lenses.desc: Where Josephus, the Gospels and Acts, and other Jewish and Christian writers tell the same events or name the same people.

sections.b:
Read it first as a Roman senator's history of one terrible year, written a generation afterward. Tacitus is interested in what power does to those who hold it, and the armies, not the Senate, now make emperors. Then read it beside the Bible's world. The same empire, provinces, officers, taxes and emperors are in Luke 2:1, Luke 3:1, Acts and the letters; the notes mark where a name is the same man (see the matches on this page) and where the likeness is only background.

Watch for three things. The Flavian side: Tacitus owed his career to Vespasian, Titus and Domitian (1:1), and the year ends with the Flavians in power. Judea at the edges: the war in Judea is first named at 1:10, Vespasian is proclaimed by the army there (2:79-81), and Book 5 turns to the Jews. Signs and gods: omens, oracles and healings run through all five books, and the notes set each beside what the Bible says about such signs.

• 9 June 68: Nero dies.
  • 15 January 69: Galba and Piso are killed; Otho is emperor (1:27-47).
  • 14 April 69: the first battle of Bedriacum; 16 April: Otho dies (Book 2). Vitellius is recognized.
  • 1 July 69: Vespasian is proclaimed at Alexandria by the legions under Tiberius Julius Alexander; Tacitus has Judea's army swear on 3 July (2:79). Josephus tells the order differently (Jewish War 4.616).
  • 24 October 69: the second battle of Bedriacum, won by Primus Antonius; Cremona is sacked (3:19-34).
  • 19 December 69: the Capitol burns (3:71-72); 20 December: Vitellius is killed; 21 December: Vespasian is recognized (Wikipedia, Year of the Four Emperors).
  • AD 70: Titus takes Jerusalem and the temple falls (Wikipedia, Titus). The Histories as we have them stop before that.

The text breaks off in the middle of a sentence at 5:26, in Civilis's speech: "I took up arms in Germany, just as Mucianus did in Syria, Aponius in Moesia and Flavianus in Pannonia". Only the first four books and the first 26 sections of the fifth survive (Wikipedia). So Tacitus's account of the end of the Batavian revolt and of the fall of Jerusalem is lost, and Josephus is the main surviving witness to the siege that Book 5 sets up. The one thing Tacitus gives of the siege is its start (5:11-13).

The Conversational English Translation is a free, idiomatic rendering in the way Americans talk today. It is made from the English of Church and Brodribb (1864), which is offered beside it as an alternate translation along with the Latin text of Fisher's Oxford Classical Text. A verse is one of Tacitus's own numbered sections, and a chapter is one of his five books. The draft was written by a local model from the English, and Claude then checked every verse against the English and the Latin; the variants record where the Latin or the base English is doubtful, and a separate reviewer checked the result. The headings in the text are the site's, not Tacitus's.

canon.summary: The Histories is a Roman history of the civil wars after Nero. It is not Scripture for any church or synagogue. It is translated here for context and read from a Christian standpoint that takes the Bible as true: it confirms much of the Bible's Roman world, and in Book 5 it gets the Jews' beginnings wrong.
accepted_by: Not a sacred book. It is a Roman writer's history, and nothing in the Perseus edition presents it as Scripture.
Read as history, not as scripture. Tacitus names what it is at 1:1: an account of the years from Galba's second consulship, by a senator whom the emperors had advanced.
Used as a main source for AD 69 with Suetonius, Plutarch, Cassius Dio and Josephus; Wikipedia's page on the year lists the ancient sources and the modern historians who work on them.
Included in the group "Other peoples and religions" as a historical work of another people, for the world around the New Testament.

provenance.b: The Latin is Charles Dennis Fisher's Oxford Classical Text (1911) and the English is the translation by Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb (1864), both from the Perseus Digital Library (Tufts University), under CC BY-SA 4.0. Five books survive, and the text breaks off in the middle of a sentence at 5:26.

The LacusCurtius introduction says the text of the Histories "depends on a single manuscript, the Mediceus II", also called Laurentianus 68, 2, which was copied in the eleventh century at Monte Cassino in Langobard script. It says that fourteen books were written and that of them only Books 1 to 4 are preserved complete, and Book 5 only to section 26. Wikipedia agrees that only the first four books and the first 26 chapters of the fifth survive. The Latin editors mark doubtful words with daggers (1:77, 3:5), and the variants record those places and the other doubtful Latin (3:5, 4:15, 4:42). This page does not trace the manuscript's later history, because nothing the writers opened tells it.
Wikipedia dates the Histories about 100-110 and the LacusCurtius introduction 104-109. The first section dates it from inside: Nerva is "divine", so he was dead, and Trajan reigned (1:1).

rejected_why.h: A Roman history, not a sacred book
rejected_why.b: The Histories does not claim to speak for God, and this site knows of no church or synagogue that treats it as Scripture. Its author writes as an outsider about the Jews, whose history he sets out at 5:2-13 and of whom he says at 5:9 that the place was "an empty seat with no image of any god inside". Its gods are the gods of Rome, and its opening verdict is that "the gods care nothing for our safety, only for punishing us" (1:3), which the Bible's God contradicts.

rejected_why.h: What the Jews and the Christians would not accept in it
rejected_why.b: Book 5 tells the origin of the Jews from Egyptian, Greek and Roman stories: a leper-exile led by Moyses, an animal image in the shrine, a Sabbath born of laziness, a hatred of outsiders (5:3-5). The Law and the prophets say the reverse, from Abraham to Moses and Sinai, and Josephus answered such tales at length in Against Apion. It is a source for what a Roman thought of the Jews, not for what the Jews believed. The Histories never names Christ or the Christians in its five books.

christian_view.b: A Christian reader takes Tacitus as a Roman historian describing the empire in which the apostles lived, and weighs what he says about Judea by the Bible's own account. Where he reports what he saw or what Roman officers did, he is a useful outside witness. Where he reports what Egyptians and Greeks said about the Jews, he is repeating an outsider's rumor, and the Bible and Josephus answer it. The notes at each verse give the check.

christian_view.h: What it confirms about the Bible's world
christian_view.b:
The names and offices of Luke and Acts are the empire's own. Tacitus's emperors include the three the Gospels and Acts name, Augustus (Luke 2:1), Tiberius (Luke 3:1) and Claudius (Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2); his Praetorian Guard and its prefects are the world of "the whole praetorium" and "Caesar's household" (Philippians 1:13; Philippians 4:22); his procurators are of the kind Pilate and Felix were, and the Roman Knights, centurions and tribunes of Acts fill his army. He names King Agrippa and Queen Berenice backing Vespasian (2:81), who are the Agrippa and Bernice of Acts 25-26; he names Felix, the governor before whom Paul was tried (5:9); and he has Herod, Pompey and the Parthian war that made Judea what it was (5:9). He tells the war in Judea as the army that Jesus' words describe: "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20). On the Jews' practices he is a witness the Law supports: circumcision, the seventh day, no pork, unleavened bread, burial, one God and no image (5:4-5; Genesis 17:11; Leviticus 11:7). And at 5:7 he preserves a Roman memory of the burned plain of the Dead Sea that matches Genesis 19:24, though he gives it a natural cause.

This does not make the Histories Scripture, and it does not prove Acts, which stands on its own witnesses. It shows that Luke's and Paul's world is the world a Roman historian describes.
christian_view.refs: Luke 2:1; Luke 3:1; Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2; Philippians 1:13; Philippians 4:22; Acts 25:13; Acts 24:24; Luke 21:20; Genesis 19:24

christian_view.h: How Roman writers saw Jews and Christians
christian_view.b:
Tacitus's chapter on the Jews (5:2-13) is an ethnography in the Greek and Roman style: origin, customs, land, history. Bloch's study, reviewed by Pieter van der Horst, finds that Tacitus follows his predecessors on the Jews in general, that even features he does not present negatively "receive a non-positive colouring," and that the impression aimed at is that the Jews fully deserved to be defeated and to have their only temple destroyed. Tacitus calls the Jewish faith "superstition" (superstitio, the Roman word for excessive, foreign religion), says that among themselves the Jews are loyal and quick to pity but feel "hostile hatred" for everyone else, and judges their rites "absurd and sordid" (5:5). The Bible answers each: the Law commands love of the foreigner, and where Jews did keep apart (Acts 10:28), keeping apart was not hatred. At the same time he notes that outsiders were drawn to the Jews' worship and gave to it (5:5), which Acts shows in God-fearers such as Cornelius (Acts 10:2).

The five books never name Christ or the Christians. Tacitus says in the Annals that "Christus" was put to death in the reign of Tiberius by the procurator Pontius Pilatus (Annals 15.44, in Church and Brodribb's wording, quoted at 5:9), and Suetonius says Claudius banished the Jews from Rome for disturbances "at the instigation of one Chrestus" (Claudius 25; see Acts 18:2). Those are the Roman glances at the new faith that we have opened here. The Histories gives no Roman view of the Christians, only of their world.

christian_view.h: Where it differs or misunderstands: Book 5
christian_view.b:
Tacitus gets the practices right and the reasons wrong. Origin: he gives five stories (Crete, Egypt, Ethiopia, Assyrian newcomers, the Solymi of Homer) and prefers the Egyptian plague and exile, not the Bible's Abraham and the Exodus. Moses: Moyses is an exile who leads a diseased crowd and invents rites opposite to all others (5:3-4); in Exodus Moses is sent by the LORD and receives the Law at Sinai (Exodus 3; Exodus 20). The shrine: he says the Jews put a statue of the animal that led them to water in the inner shrine (5:4), then says elsewhere that they put up no statues and that the sanctuary held no image (5:5, 5:9). On the empty inmost room 5:9 and Josephus agree: he puts the gold furniture in the outer sanctuary and says of the inmost room, "In this there was nothing at all" (Jewish War 5.5.5). The Sabbath: laziness, or a feast of Saturn (5:4), not rest from labor (Exodus 20:8-11). Persons: he calls John "Bargioras" (5:12), mixing John of Gischala with Simon son of Gioras (Josephus), and has Varus punish the rebel Simon where Josephus has Gratus (5:9). The oracle: he says the old writing of the priests that men from Judea would rule the world pointed to Vespasian and Titus (5:13). A Christian reads the promise of a ruler for all peoples (Genesis 49:10; Numbers 24:17; Daniel 7:13-14) as fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 2:2; Luke 1:33).

Where Christians differ on the Sabbath, on images and on oaths and war, which Book 5, Book 4 and Book 3 raise, the chapter pages set out the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist and other views side by side.

christian_view.h: The healings at Alexandria, and the Gospels
christian_view.b:
At 4:81 Tacitus tells that while Vespasian waited at Alexandria for the summer winds, a man blind in his eyes begged him, on the advice of the god Serapis, to wet his eyes with spit, and a man with a diseased hand asked to have it stepped on. Vespasian laughed, then asked the doctors, who said the sight and the joints could be restored, and he did it: "At once the hand was turned back to use, and daylight shone again for the blind man." Tacitus adds that those present still tell it "now that there is nothing to gain from lying." Suetonius (Vespasian 7.2-3) and Cassius Dio tell it too. Josephus says nothing of it.

Three readings are open, and the notes at 4:81 give them. John Meier, as quoted by John Dickson, reads it as a staged "photo opportunity" that gave a general without a clear claim some legitimacy, and Dickson thinks it probably a fraud. Eric Eve argues that Mark added spit to the Bethsaida story (Mark 8:23) to allude to Vespasian's and set Jesus against Rome, which needs a Mark written after AD 69. Tacitus's own doctors suggest an ordinary recovery. A Christian reader notes the differences: in the Gospels, Jesus consults no doctor and asks for no audience (Mark 8:23; Mark 8:26), and the apostles' witnesses paid for what they said (Acts 5:40-41). Matthew 24:24 and 2 Thessalonians 2:9 warn that signs and wonders can serve falsehood, and Deuteronomy 13:1-3 says to test a sign by what it asks you to worship. Whether the Gospel stories answer Rome's is argued; this page does not decide it.

christian_view.h: The burning of the Capitol, and the fall of the temple
christian_view.b: Tacitus calls the burning of the Capitol "the saddest and most shameful thing to happen to the Roman republic since the city was founded" (3:72). The Capitol was Rome's holy hill, and the temple on it a "pledge of empire". The ancient accounts differ on who lit it (3:71). The next year Jerusalem's temple fell to Titus's army. Jesus had said of the temple buildings, "Here not one stone will be left on a stone. Every one will be knocked down" (Mark 13:2; see also Matthew 24:2). This page does not say that AD 70 is the only event that saying can mean. Josephus dates the temple's burning to the tenth of Lous, the day it was burned by the king of Babylon (Jewish War 6.4.5). The two holy hills are set side by side in the notes: the Capitol was rebuilt on the same footprint and dedicated in AD 75 (4:53), and Vespasian turned the Jewish temple tax into a payment to Jupiter Capitolinus (Josephus, Jewish War 7.218). Tacitus does not link the two events. See the spec box on this page.

Luke 3:1: Tacitus's "Tiberius Nero, his stepson" is the emperor of the fifteenth year (1:15), and his one line on Judea under Tiberius is "Under Tiberius it was quiet" (5:9), the years of John and Jesus. He does not name Pilate in the Histories. Acts: Claudius, Felix, Drusilla, Agrippa, Bernice and the praetorium all have their Roman side here, with the Roman barracks beside the temple (Acts 21:31-37; see the note at 5:11); Nero is the Caesar of Paul's appeal (Acts 25:11). Revelation: the rumor that Nero had not died, and the pretender caught at Cythnus (2:8), are read by some as the background of the beast whose wound healed (Revelation 13:3); others read the beast as the empire or an end-time ruler. Readers count the seven kings of Revelation 17:10 from Julius Caesar, from Augustus, or skipping the three short reigns of AD 68-69 (3:68), and the count changes the date of Revelation. Many place it under Domitian, whom Tacitus shows as a young Caesar in 69 (4:2). Josephus: he tells the same year in short form (Jewish War 4) and the same war from inside, so each fills gaps in the other; the notes line up where they agree and differ.

The questions that Atrahasis raises, whether one text borrowed from another, do not apply in the same way. The Histories was written after the events, from the Roman side, and does not claim to speak for God. The questions that do apply are the ones this page takes in turn: how Romans saw Jews and Christians, whether an outsider's report carries weight where it agrees with the Bible, and where it bends the Bible's world.

christian_view.h: Do the gods care? Rulers and the Bible's answer
christian_view.b: Tacitus's verdict on his age is that "the gods care nothing for our safety, only for punishing us" (1:3). Jesus says that not one sparrow falls without the Father (Matthew 10:29-31), and God says, "I take no pleasure in the death of a wicked man" (Ezekiel 33:11). On rulers, the Bible tells Christians to pray for those in power (1 Timothy 2:1-2) and to honor the king (1 Peter 2:17), even for emperors like these, and "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). Tacitus shows two ways of living under a bad ruler in the Senate after Vitellius's fall, in Helvidius Priscus and Eprius Marcellus (4:5-8).

cited_in.b: Augustus, the first emperor. Luke has "an order came out from Caesar Augustus"; Tacitus names the "divine Augustus" among the emperors whose reigns he recalls (1:15) and the Senate gives Otho the same title (1:47). Same man.
Tiberius, in whose fifteenth year John began. Tacitus's one line on Judea in those years is "Under Tiberius it was quiet" (5:9).
The siege of Jerusalem by Roman armies. Tacitus has the army, the camp and the earthworks of the siege (5:11-13); his account of its end is lost. Josephus tells it in full.
The burning of the Capitol (19 December 69) and the temple's fall a year later (see the spec box). Tacitus does not link them.
Claudius, in whose days the famine Agabus foretold came. Tacitus names Claudius in the speech to Vitellius (3:66) and in the story of Judea under procurators (5:9).
Claudius's order that the Jews leave Rome. Suetonius (Claudius 25) dates the disturbances to "one Chrestus"; Tacitus's Claudius gives Judea to Roman Knights and freedmen (5:9).
The death of Herod Agrippa I at Caesarea. Tacitus says Claudius gave Judea to Knights and freedmen after the kings were dead or cut down to little (5:9).
Paphos, where Paul met the proconsul Sergius Paulus. Tacitus describes the temple of Venus there and Titus's visit (2:2-4). The two texts share the place only; Sergius Paulus is not in Tacitus.
The Roman barracks beside the temple where Paul was taken. Josephus names it the Antonia (Jewish War 5.5.8); Tacitus describes the temple fortress and the walls (5:11-12).
Felix, the governor before whom Paul was tried, with Drusilla. Tacitus's Felix is "Antonius Felix" who "exercised a king's power with a slave's mind" (5:9). See the matches.
King Agrippa and Bernice at Paul's hearing. Tacitus has Agrippa and Berenice backing Vespasian (2:81); Agrippa sails with Titus in Josephus (Jewish War 4.9.2). Same people; see the matches.
Paul's appeal to Caesar, which means Nero's court although the verse does not name him. Tacitus names Nero throughout Book 1.
"The whole praetorium": the Praetorian Guard enters the story at 1:5 and again at 4:2. The site's Philippians page sets out the views (the guard in Rome, or a governor's headquarters).

A blind man healed with spit. The Alexandria story has the same elements (spit, a blind man) in a different setting; Eric Eve argues that Mark's story alludes to it. See "The healings at Alexandria, and the Gospels".
Herod the Great, king of Judea at Jesus' birth. Tacitus says Antony gave him the kingdom and Augustus enlarged it (5:9).

The rumor that Nero was alive and the pretender caught at Cythnus (2:8; 1:2). Some readers hear this behind the beast whose wound healed; others read the beast as the empire or an end-time ruler. Tacitus does not mention Christians.

The seven kings and the short reigns of AD 68-69. Tacitus lists the ends of Caesar, Gaius, Nero, Piso and Galba (3:68); how readers count from Julius Caesar or Augustus changes the date of Revelation. Tacitus does not mention Revelation.
Antiochus's ban on the Law and the abomination that desolates. Tacitus has "King Antiochus tried to strip away their superstition and give them Greek ways" (5:8). Same event, opposite verdict.
The fire on the plain of Sodom. Tacitus has the rich plain, the cities and fire from the sky, and gives his own reason for the barren land (5:7).
Water from a rock in the wilderness. Tacitus's Moyses follows wild asses to a rock and opens veins of water; the rest of his story reverses Exodus (5:3).

matches.name: Antonius Felix, the governor of Judea (5:9)
matches.bible: Felix, the governor before whom Paul is tried (Acts 23-24)
matches.b:
For: Tacitus says that Claudius handed the province of Judea to Roman Knights or freedmen: "One of them, Antonius Felix, using every kind of cruelty and lust, exercised a king's power with a slave's mind" (5:9). Josephus says "Claudius sent Felix, the brother of Pallas, to take care of the affairs of Judea" (Antiquities 20.7.1), and in the Annals the Felix of Judea is the brother of Pallas (Annals 12.54). Suetonius lists Felix among Claudius's freedmen, says Claudius made him governor of Judea and that he became "the husband of three queens" (Claudius 28); Annals 12.53 calls Pallas, whom Annals 12.54 names as Felix's brother, a freedman. Acts has Lysias send Paul "through safely to Felix, the governor" (Acts 23:24), Paul tells him that he has "sat as judge over this nation for many years" (Acts 24:10), and after two full years Porcius Festus took over (Acts 24:27). William Whiston's note to Antiquities 20.7.2 treats Tacitus's Felix as the same man as Josephus's.

Against: one difference in order. Annals 12.54 has Felix already governing Samaria while Cumanus governs Galilee, whereas Josephus sends Felix after Claudius banishes Cumanus (Antiquities 20.6.3, 20.7.1). The offices and the family tie agree. Tacitus's wife for Felix (Drusilla, granddaughter of Cleopatra and Antony) is not the Drusilla of Acts; see the next match.

Verdict: very likely the same man. Another Felix in the Histories, Sextilius Felix (3:5), is a different officer; see below.

matches.name: Drusilla, Felix's wife (5:9)
matches.bible: Drusilla, Felix's wife (Acts 24:24)
matches.b:
For: Acts has Felix come "with Drusilla, his own wife, a Jewish woman" (Acts 24:24). Josephus says this Drusilla was a sister of Agrippa II who had married Azizus, king of Emesa; Felix fell in love with her and sent a Cypriot Jew named Simon to persuade her to leave her husband, and she married Felix and had a son Agrippa (Antiquities 20.7.1-2). Tacitus has Felix marry Drusilla, "granddaughter of Cleopatra and Antony" (5:9). The names match, and Whiston's note on Antiquities 20.7.2 holds that Felix did marry a granddaughter of Antony and Cleopatra, as Tacitus says, and that Tacitus mistook the Jewish Drusilla for that other wife, whose name he did not know.

Against: the ancestry Tacitus gives is not the Jewish princess's. Suetonius says Felix was "the husband of three queens" (Claudius 28), and footnote 537 in the Thomson-Forester English of Suetonius holds that two of Felix's wives were named Drusilla, the Jewish sister of Agrippa in Acts 24:24 and a granddaughter of Cleopatra by Antony. Whiston and the Suetonius editors are two sources for the same two-wives reading, not rival views. The Book 5 notes judge that view the likeliest, and say that nothing in Tacitus contradicts Acts, since he never says who Felix's wife was in the 50s.

Verdict: possible that Tacitus's Drusilla is the Drusilla of Acts, with a confusion in Tacitus; the two-wives view is the likelier. This is the site's judgment from the texts.

matches.name: Agrippa, the king (1:10 through Josephus; 2:81; 4:39; 5:1)
matches.bible: King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II), who heard Paul (Acts 25-26)
matches.b:
For: Tacitus has Agrippa called away from Rome by secret messages and hurrying across the sea to join Vespasian (2:81), thanked among "the allied kings" (4:39), and in Titus's army in the year 70 (5:1). Josephus has "king Agrippa" sail with Titus toward Galba (Jewish War 4.9.2) and says Claudius gave the younger Agrippa the territory of Philip and other lands and that he had sisters Drusilla and Bernice (Antiquities 20.7.1). Acts has "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13), and Paul speaks before him (Acts 26). His father, Agrippa I, died at Caesarea (Acts 12:23).

Against: nothing. Only one king Agrippa was reigning in AD 70.

Verdict: very likely the same man, Herod Agrippa II. Fonteius Agrippa (3:46) is a Roman senator and a different man.

matches.name: Berenice, the queen (2:2; 2:81; 3:47; 4:39)
matches.bible: Bernice, Agrippa's sister (Acts 25:13, 25:23, 26:30)
matches.b:
For: Tacitus says Berenice backed Vespasian "with no less spirit" than the kings (2:81) and that Titus was said to have turned back for love of her (2:2). Acts spells her name Bernice and has her arrive with Agrippa "in grand display" at Paul's hearing (Acts 25:23). Josephus names her as Agrippa I's daughter and Agrippa II's sister (Antiquities 20.7.1, 20.7.3) and tells of her marriage to Polemon (Antiquities 20.145-146). Suetonius says Titus later sent her away from Rome (Titus 7). The name (Bernice is the Greek form, Berenice the Latin), rank, family and time all match.

Against: nothing in the identity. Acts never mentions her tie to Titus; Tacitus gives it as what "some believed" and says it did not hinder his business (2:2).

Verdict: very likely the same woman.

matches.name: Polemon, king of Pontus and Cilicia (3:47)
matches.bible: Polemon, the husband of Berenice (outside the Bible; Josephus, Antiquities 20.145-146)
matches.b:
For: Josephus says Berenice "persuaded Poleme, who was king of Cilicia, to be circumcised, and to marry her", that the marriage did not last, "Bernice left Poleme, and, as was said, with impure intentions", and that he "forsook at once this matrimony, and the Jewish religion" (Antiquities 20.145-146; Whiston 20.7.3). Tacitus says Anicetus, a freedman of Polemon and once commander of the royal fleet, raised Pontus for Vitellius after the kingdom "was turned into a province" (3:47), and Suetonius says Nero added "the realm of Pontus, when it was given up by Polemon" (Nero 18). A king Polemon who gave up Pontus to Rome and a king Poleme of Cilicia who married Berenice are the same man if one king held both; a Wikipedia page on Polemon II says he ruled Pontus and Cilicia, married Berenice and abandoned Judaism.

Against: Tacitus does not mention the marriage or Berenice in this passage, and names Polemon only as the former master of Anicetus. The Wikipedia page does not mention Tacitus 3:47. The identification rests on Suetonius, Josephus and Tacitus's own words "Polemonis libertus", read together, not on a source that joins them.

Verdict: likely the same man. Acts names Bernice at Agrippa's side (Acts 25:13) but does not name Polemon.

matches.name: Herod the Great (5:9)
matches.bible: Herod, king of Judea at Jesus' birth (Matthew 2; Luke 1:5)
matches.b:
For: Tacitus's Herod, whose kingdom Antony gave him and whom Augustus enlarged after his victory (5:9), is Herod the Great, the king of Judea in Matthew 2:1 and Luke 1:5. The Gospels' Herod is "alarmed" at the news of a newborn king (Matthew 2:3). Tacitus's Antony and Augustus are also the background of "an order came out from Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1). After Herod's death the realm was ruled in three parts by his children (5:9); Matthew names Archelaus and Luke 3:1 names Herod and Philip.

Against: nothing.

Verdict: very likely the same man.
matches.refs: Matthew 2:1; Matthew 2:3; Matthew 2:22; Luke 1:5; Luke 2:1; Luke 3:1

matches.name: Moyses (5:3)
matches.bible: Moses
matches.b:
For: the name, Egypt, the wilderness, the water from a rock and the laws all line up, and Josephus treats the Egyptian Osarsiph and Moyses stories as slanders about Moses (Against Apion 1.26-31). Strabo also calls Moses an Egyptian priest (Geography 16.2.35).

Against: the story is not the Bible's. In Exodus Moses is a Hebrew raised in Pharaoh's house who flees to Midian (Exodus 2:15-22) and is sent back by the LORD (Exodus 3); he does not arise as an exile from a plague camp, and his laws come from God at Sinai (Exodus 20), not from a plan "to make sure of the nation's loyalty" (5:4).

Verdict: very likely the same person, told by outsiders in a distorted and hostile story. The Egyptian-priest tradition could be friendly or hostile (Strabo's is friendly).

matches.name: King Antiochus (5:8)
matches.bible: Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who banned the Law (1 Maccabees 1; Daniel 11)
matches.b:
For: Tacitus says "King Antiochus tried to strip away their superstition and give them Greek ways", but that the war with the Parthians kept him from changing this "vilest of nations" (5:8). 1 Maccabees has the king write that each was to give up his own customs and says they built an abomination of desolation on the altar (1 Maccabees 1:42, 1:54), and Daniel foretold "the abomination that desolates" (Daniel 11:31). Same event, opposite verdict.

Against: Tacitus gives no number or epithet, and the identification rests on the king's act. 1 Maccabees is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches and is not accepted by Jews or most Protestants.

Verdict: likely the same king, Antiochus IV.

matches.name: Pompey (1:15; 2:38; 5:9)
matches.bible: Pompey, who took Jerusalem in 63 BC (not named in the Bible)
matches.b:
For: Tacitus says Gnaeus Pompeius "was the first Roman to conquer the Jews, and by right of victory he went into the temple" (5:9). Josephus tells how Pompey took the temple area and entered the sanctuary (Jewish War 1.7.6), and the Roman rule under which the Jews lived in Jesus' day came from that. The site's topic on Rome gives the date.

Against: nothing in the two accounts. Tacitus says the seat was empty of any image of a god (5:9). Josephus says Pompey saw the gold lampstand, table, vessels and censers and touched none of it (Jewish War 1.7.6), and that the furniture stood in the outer sanctuary while the inmost room held "nothing at all" (Jewish War 5.5.5), so the two agree. The Bible does not name Pompey.

Verdict: very likely the same man in Tacitus and Josephus.

matches.name: Augustus (1:15; 1:47; 3:66; 5:9)
matches.bible: Caesar Augustus (Luke 2:1)
matches.b: Tacitus's "divine Augustus", who won at Actium and did not leave Antony alive (3:66), is the first emperor, and Luke's "Caesar Augustus" is that man. The Senate votes the same title to Otho (1:47). Verdict: very likely, as far as certainty goes.

matches.name: Tiberius (1:15; 5:9)
matches.bible: Tiberius Caesar (Luke 3:1)
matches.b: Tacitus's "Tiberius Nero, his stepson", whom Augustus made his heir (1:15), is the Tiberius of "the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule" (Luke 3:1). Verdict: very likely.

matches.name: Claudius (1:16; 3:66; 5:9)
matches.bible: Claudius (Acts 11:28; 18:2)
matches.b: Claudius is named in Acts for the famine in his days (Acts 11:28) and for the order that all the Jews leave Rome (Acts 18:2). Tacitus's Claudius is the emperor who handed Judea to Knights and freedmen (5:9), and the Claudius of the colony Colonia Agrippinensis (4:28). Verdict: very likely, the same emperor.

matches.name: Nero (1:5; 1:78; 2:8)
matches.bible: The Caesar to whom Paul appealed (Acts 25:11); the emperor of Acts 28:16
matches.b: For: Acts does not name him; Paul says "I appeal to Caesar!" (Acts 25:11). By the dates, Paul's appeal and his custody in Rome fall in Nero's reign (AD 54-68, Tacitus's emperor in Book 1). Against: no text in Acts says "Nero". Verdict: very likely by the dates. Whether Revelation 13:3 or 17:10 refers to him is a separate question (see the match on the false Nero).

matches.name: Vespasian (1:1; 1:10; 2:78-81)
matches.bible: Vespasian, the general of the Jewish war (not named in the Bible; Josephus, Jewish War 3.1.2-3; 4.9.2)
matches.b: Tacitus's Vespasian, whom Nero had chosen for Judea (1:10), is Josephus's Vespasian, whom Nero found "equal to the task" and sent to Syria. He is the commander of the war that ended with Jerusalem's fall (Luke 21:20 speaks of Jerusalem encircled by army camps). Josephus also records that Vespasian freed him after he predicted the throne (Jewish War 4.10). Verdict: very likely the same man; the Bible does not name him.

matches.name: Titus, Vespasian's son (1:1; 5:1; 5:10-13)
matches.bible: Titus, who took Jerusalem (not named in the Bible; Josephus, Jewish War 3.1.1-3; 4.9.2)
matches.b: Tacitus's Titus, Vespasian's son, whom he sends to end the war in Judea (4:51; 5:1), is Josephus's Titus, who sailed to Galba with Agrippa and turned back (Jewish War 4.9.2) and was later sent to destroy Jerusalem (Jewish War 4.11.5). The siege that followed is the kind of event Jesus spoke of (Luke 21:20; Matthew 24:2). Verdict: very likely the same man.

matches.name: Titus, Vespasian's son, and Paul's Titus (2:86; 4:51)
matches.bible: Titus, Paul's co-worker (2 Timothy 4:10; Galatians 2:3; 2 Corinthians 8:23)
matches.b: At 2:86 Tacitus's Dalmatia is a war zone in AD 69, and Paul says in his last letter that Titus went "to Dalmatia" (2 Timothy 4:10). Paul's Titus was "a Greek" convert (Galatians 2:3) and "my partner and my fellow worker" (2 Corinthians 8:23). Vespasian's son was a general in Judea and later emperor, and Titus was a common name. Verdict: unlikely that they are one man.

matches.name: Tiberius Alexander (1:11; 2:74; 4:81)
matches.bible: Tiberius Alexander (Josephus; the sons of Judas the Galilean, Acts 5:37, are named in his story)
matches.b:
For: Tacitus's Tiberius Alexander, a native of Egypt who governed it and had the legions swear to Vespasian (1:11; 2:74), shares name, province and role with Josephus's Tiberius Alexander, son of the alabarch Alexander of Alexandria, who "did not continue in the religion of his country", followed Cuspius Fadus as procurator of Judea and ordered James and Simon, sons of Judas the Galilean, crucified (Jewish War 2.11.6; Antiquities 20.5.2). He held back a Jewish riot at Alexandria (Jewish War 2.18.7) and had the legions swear (Jewish War 4.10.6). Wikipedia names Philo as his uncle.

Against: nothing. The Bible does not name him; Acts 5:37 names his victims' father.

Verdict: very likely the same man in Tacitus and Josephus; no New Testament name found for him.

matches.name: Quintilius Varus (4:17; 5:9)
matches.bible: Varus, president of Syria in the last years of Herod the Great (not named in the Bible; Josephus)
matches.b: Civilis recalls Varus, who lost his army to the Germans (AD 9) (4:17). Tacitus says the Varus who held Syria after Herod's death punished a rebel Simon (5:9). Josephus names "Varus, the president of Syria" at Herod the Great's last trial of his son (Jewish War 1.31.5). Wikipedia's article on Publius Quinctilius Varus holds that the Syrian governor (about 7 to 4 BC) and the commander lost in AD 9 are one man. The Bible never names him, but Joseph's dream-warning about Herod's son Archelaus (Matthew 2:19-22) falls in the years just after his governorship. Velleius Paterculus says of Varus in Syria that "he entered this rich province a poor man, and left this poor province a rich man" (2.117.2, Shipley's translation at Livius.org). Josephus has Gratus, not Varus, kill the rebel Simon (Jewish War 2.4.2); the rebel is not the Simon of any Bible book. Verdict: very likely the same man in all three texts.

matches.name: Gaius (Caligula) (4:15; 5:9)
matches.bible: Gaius, who ordered his statue set up in the temple (not named in this site's Gospels and Acts; Josephus, Jewish War 2.10.1)
matches.b: Tacitus says the Jews, ordered by Caligula to put his statue in the temple, took up arms rather than do it (5:9). Josephus tells the same event, with Petronius meeting Jews at Ptolemais (Jewish War 2.10.1-3). The site's Gospels and Acts name only Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius among the emperors (the writers checked); some readers hear Caligula's plan behind the "abomination of desolation" of Mark 13:14. Verdict: very likely the same emperor and event in Tacitus and Josephus.

matches.name: Lucilius Bassus (2:100; 3:12; 4:3)
matches.bible: Lucilius Bassus, legate in Judea (outside the Bible; Josephus, Jewish War 7.6.1). He took Herodium, which Josephus says Herod built (Jewish War 1.21.10); Matthew 2:1 names only King Herod
matches.b: Tacitus first names this Bassus as a cavalry commander whom Vitellius made prefect of the fleets at Ravenna and Misenum (2:100); he turned the Ravenna fleet to Vespasian (3:12; 3:36), and at 4:3 the new government sends a Lucilius Bassus with light cavalry to settle Campania. Josephus has "Lucilius Bassus" sent "as legate into Judea" after Titus left, where he took the citadel at Herodium (Jewish War 7.6.1). The name, the date and a commander the Flavians trusted all fit, and Josephus says Herod built and named Herodium (Jewish War 1.21.10). Wikipedia's article on Lucilius Bassus treats the Ravenna-fleet prefect and the Judean legate as one man without an argument and cites no passage for it. Verdict: likely, from the name, the date and the Flavian trust; no ancient text states the identity. Matthew 2:1 names only King Herod.

matches.name: Epiphanes (2:25)
matches.bible: King Epiphanes, son of Antiochus IV of Commagene (Josephus, Jewish War 5.11.3)
matches.b: Tacitus names only "King Epiphanes", loyal to Otho. The Wikipedia article on Antiochus IV of Commagene (Tacitus's Antiochus at 2:81, "the richest of the subject kings") says his son was named Epiphanes and led troops to help Titus at Jerusalem, citing Josephus. Tacitus does not give this king's land or father. Verdict: possible that it is the same man. The Bible does not name him.

matches.name: Basilides (2:78; 4:82)
matches.bible: Basilides the priest at Carmel and the Egyptian notable at Alexandria (outside the Bible; Suetonius, Vespasian 7.1)
matches.b: At Carmel the priest Basilides examines the entrails and tells Vespasian he will get "a great dwelling, huge boundaries, and many men" (2:78). In Book 4 a Basilides, one of the leading Egyptians, appears to Vespasian in the temple of Serapis though he is days away (4:82). Suetonius gives that vision to a freedman Basilides (Vespasian 7.1). Verdict: possible but unproven that they are one man; the name is common, the places are far apart, and Tacitus does not link them. Carmel is Elijah's mountain (1 Kings 18).

matches.name: Seleucus, the astrologer (2:78; 1:22)
matches.bible: Seleucus, the astrologer Suetonius gives to Otho (outside the Bible)
matches.b: Tacitus says that, as master of the world, Vespasian openly kept one Seleucus, an astrologer, to direct his counsels (2:78). Tacitus gives Otho a different astrologer, Ptolemaeus, who had foretold in Spain that Otho would survive Nero (1:22). Suetonius, Otho 4, names Seleucus as the astrologer who promised Otho he would outlive Nero and later that he would be emperor, and the editor's note there says Tacitus and Plutarch give Ptolemaeus as the name. Verdict: possible that Tacitus's Seleucus, Vespasian's adviser, is the man Suetonius places with Otho; neither writer says so. The Bible condemns reliance on astrologers (Isaiah 47:13).

matches.name: The Flavian-era writers (2:101)
matches.bible: Josephus, who wrote the Jewish War after Vespasian freed him
matches.b: Tacitus says the writers who recorded this war while the Flavian house was in power wrote of "concern for peace and love of the state" to flatter (2:101). He names none. Josephus wrote the Jewish War, which tells these months, after Vespasian freed him (Jewish War 4.10). The charge fits Josephus as well as any Roman author, but Tacitus does not name him and no source opened for this page makes the link. Verdict: possible. This is a Claude idea.

matches.name: The false Nero (1:2; 2:8)
matches.bible: The beast whose death wound was healed (Revelation 13:3; 17:11)
matches.b: Tacitus is an early witness to the rumor that Nero had not died: a pretender, a slave or freedman who looked and sang like Nero, was caught at Cythnus and killed (2:8), and the Parthians were nearly fooled by a fake Nero (1:2). Some readers of Revelation connect the rumor to the beast whose "death wound was healed" and to an eighth king who "belongs to the seven". Others read the beast as the empire or an end-time ruler. Tacitus does not mention Christians. Verdict: possible as background, not proven.

matches.name: The ruler from Judea (2:1; 5:13)
matches.bible: The promised ruler: Genesis 49:10; Numbers 24:17; Daniel 7:13-14
matches.b: Tacitus, Josephus and Suetonius report an ancient saying that men setting out from Judea would rule the world, and give it to Vespasian and Titus (5:13; Jewish War 6.5.4; Vespasian 4). None names a verse. Candidates are Genesis 49:10, Numbers 24:17 and Daniel 7:13-14. A Christian reads these of Jesus, "the newborn king of the Jews" (Matthew 2:2). Verdict: possible that the saying rests on one of these verses; the choice among them is a guess.

matches.name: Mount Carmel's altar (2:78)
matches.bible: Elijah's altar on Carmel (1 Kings 18:30-32)
matches.b: Tacitus says the ancestors of the locals handed down that the god of Carmel has no statue or temple, only an altar. Elijah "mended the LORD's altar, which had been knocked down" and built an altar of twelve stones (1 Kings 18:30-32). The bare altar could be an echo of this by way of local memory. Against it: an inscription to Zeus of Carmel shows a Greek-style god worshiped there (Wikipedia), and Tacitus says nothing of Elijah or Israel. Verdict: possible, unproven. This is a Claude idea.

matches.name: Sextilius Felix (3:5)
matches.bible: Felix, the governor (Acts 24:27)
matches.b: Sextilius Felix commands a cavalry wing, eight cohorts and the levy of Noricum on the river Aenus (3:5). Felix was a common name, he is an army officer on the Danube side, and the governor of Judea is Tacitus's Antonius Felix in Book 5. Verdict: unlikely; no source opened ties them.

matches.name: Fonteius Agrippa (3:46)
matches.bible: King Agrippa (Acts 25:13)
matches.b: Tacitus calls Fonteius Agrippa a proconsul of Asia (3:46). He is a Roman senator and the king is a Jewish ruler; the name Agrippa is shared. Verdict: unlikely.

matches.name: Julius Agrestis (3:54)
matches.bible: Julius, the centurion of the Emperor's Cohort (Acts 27:1)
matches.b: Agrestis is a Vitellianist centurion in AD 69 who goes to Antonius's camp and back. Acts has Paul turned over "to a centurion of the Emperor's Cohort, a man named Julius" (Acts 27:1). Julius was one of the commonest Roman names, and the two men serve different commanders. Verdict: unlikely.

matches.name: Cornelius Martialis (3:70)
matches.bible: Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian Cohort (Acts 10:1)
matches.b: Martialis carries Sabinus's message to Vitellius and is cut down on the Capitol (3:70; 3:73). Cornelius was a common family name; the Cornelius of Acts is at Caesarea in Judea. Verdict: unlikely.

matches.name: Valerius Festus (4:49)
matches.bible: Porcius Festus, the governor (Acts 24:27; 25:10-12)
matches.b: Tacitus's Festus is Valerius Festus, legate of the legion in Africa in AD 69 to 70, whom Tacitus calls "a young man". Porcius Festus "took over from Felix" years before AD 70. The family names and the posts differ. Verdict: unlikely.

matches.name: Claudia Sacrata (5:22)
matches.bible: Claudia (2 Timothy 4:21)
matches.b: Claudia Sacrata is an Ubian woman, Cerialis's alleged companion (5:22). 2 Timothy 4:21 sends greetings from "Eubulus, from Pudens, Linus and Claudia". Claudia was a very common woman's name, the women live on different edges of the empire, and nothing but the name links them. Verdict: unlikely.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what a Roman senator of about AD 100 thought of the year 69 and of the Jews, the Histories is excellent: he wrote it himself, in his own language, a generation after the events, and he says where he owes debts. As a text it survives in one medieval manuscript and breaks off at 5:26, so what is lost includes the siege of Jerusalem. As history it is sound on the Roman events and checks out against Josephus and Suetonius in outline; where it describes the Jews it repeats outsiders' stories and gets origins and reasons wrong. As theology, measured by the Bible, it gets the facts of the Jewish customs right and the meaning wrong: its gods only punish, its Jews are an odd and hateful people, and its signs serve the Flavians.

sections.h: 1. A witness to what its first hearers believed: very high, for Roman readers
sections.b: We do not have to guess how a Roman senator of the early second century saw the civil wars, the army, the Senate and the Jews: this is his own history. It shows the ranks and offices (Praetorian Guard, procurators, Roman Knights), omens, oaths and the habit of reading signs, and a Roman's sneer at a foreign religion. Two cautions. Tacitus owed his career to the Flavians (1:1), and Wikipedia says the experience of Domitian's reign left him "jaded and perhaps ashamed at his own complicity," with a hatred of tyranny evident in his works; the historian Brian Jones argues that the shared bias of the writers on Domitian makes his true character hard to judge. The Jews' chapter is a Roman ethnography, not a Jewish source (Bloch, reviewed by van der Horst).

sections.h: 2. Textual reliability: one medieval copy, and a stop in the middle of a sentence
sections.b: The surviving text depends on one manuscript, the Second Medicean (Laurentianus 68, 2), copied in the eleventh century at Monte Cassino, about a thousand years after the events (LacusCurtius introduction). Only Books 1 to 4 and the first 26 sections of Book 5 survive, out of fourteen books by the same introduction. Where the Latin is doubtful the editors mark it with daggers (1:77, 3:5), and the variants list those places and the cruxes at 4:15 and 4:42. One copy means no second witness to settle a disputed word, so each variant says what the Conversational English Translation follows and why. The text of the Jews' chapter is intact. The lost parts include his account of the siege of Jerusalem and the end of the Batavian revolt.

sections.h: 3. As history: sound on Rome, one-sided on the Jews
sections.b: On the main events of AD 69, Tacitus agrees with Suetonius, Plutarch and Josephus and differs on details: the number who first hailed Otho (23 in Tacitus and Plutarch, fifteen in Suetonius), Otho's astrologer (Ptolemaeus in Tacitus 1:22, and in Plutarch by the editor's note to Suetonius, Otho 4; Seleucus in Suetonius, whom Tacitus gives to Vespasian at 2:78), who lit the Capitol (3:71), the order of Vespasian's proclamation (Tacitus: Alexandria on 1 July, Judea on 3 July; Josephus has Judea first), Vitellius's age (3:86). On Judea he differs from Josephus in two places: Josephus has Gratus, not Varus, kill the rebel Simon (Jewish War 2.4.2), and John and Simon son of Gioras are two men in Josephus, where Tacitus gives John the name "Bargioras" (5:12). On the temple the two agree: Pompey found no image of a god in the inmost room (5:9), and Josephus puts the furniture in the outer sanctuary and says the inmost room held "nothing at all" (Jewish War 5.5.5). Josephus answers the Egyptian stories of the Jews in Against Apion. Tacitus names few sources and calls others "most writers" (5:3). Measured by the Bible, his history of Judea gets the Roman framework (Pompey, Herod, Augustus, the procurators, Felix, the Jewish War) right and the Jews' own history wrong. The Alexandria healings are told by three Roman-era writers; whether they were staged, natural or something more is argued (see the christian view above).

sections.h: 4. As theology, measured by the Bible
sections.b:
• Agrees: the Jews of his day keep circumcision (Genesis 17:11), the seventh day (Exodus 20:8-11), no pork (Leviticus 11:7), unleavened bread (Exodus 12:34), burial, one God known by the mind and no image of him (Deuteronomy 6:4; Exodus 20:4); the fire from the sky on the plain of Sodom (Genesis 19:24); the war in Judea is the army Jesus described (Luke 21:20); a ruler from Judea was widely expected (Genesis 49:10; Numbers 24:17).
  • Goes beyond: Roman omens, oracles, the healing at Alexandria and the god Serapis, which the Bible does not tell; the Bible says only that signs can serve falsehood (Matthew 24:24; 2 Thessalonians 2:9) and must be tested by what they ask you to worship (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).
  • Conflicts: the gods only punish (1:3; Matthew 10:29-31; Ezekiel 33:11); the Jews' origin as an Egyptian leper-exile led by Moyses, who made rites opposite to everyone else's (5:3-4; Exodus 3; Exodus 20); an animal image in the inner shrine (5:4; Exodus 20:4); the Sabbath as laziness (5:4; Exodus 20:8-11); and the oracle given to Vespasian and Titus in place of the promised ruler (5:13; Matthew 2:2). On each of these the site takes the Bible's side while describing Tacitus fairly. Where Christians differ among themselves, on the Sabbath, images, oaths and war, the chapter pages set out each view.

how_to_read.b: This is a Roman history, not Scripture, and no church has treated it as Scripture. It is here to show the world the New Testament was written in, and what a Roman writer said about Judea.

how_to_read.h: Chapters and verses are Tacitus's books and sections
how_to_read.b: Chapter 1 is Tacitus's Book 1, and verse 1:4 is his Book 1, section 4. The book ends in the middle of a sentence at 5:26, because the Histories survive only that far. The headings in the text are the site's.

The matches on this page list every person, king, governor, place and event that the Histories shares with the Bible or with Josephus, with how sure each match is: very likely, likely, possible or unlikely. Where the match is only a shared name, the verdict says so.
The Conversational English Translation is a free modern rendering. Switch to Church and Brodribb or to the Latin to see the words it came from.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a pair of fires
spec.body: Tacitus calls the burning of the Capitol on 19 December 69 "the saddest and most shameful thing to happen to the Roman republic since the city was founded" (3:72). The Jerusalem temple burned the next year (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5), and Jesus had said of the temple buildings, "Here not one stone will be left on a stone. Every one will be knocked down" (Mark 13:2). A Jew or Christian reading Tacitus could set the two losses side by side, and Vespasian then ordered every Jew to pay to the Capitol the two drachmae they had paid to the temple (Josephus, Jewish War 7.218). The two fires, however, came from opposite sides of the civil war: Josephus has the soldiers "that came from Germany", for Vitellius, take the Capitol hill and set the temple on fire (Jewish War 4.11.4), while Vespasian, who won, sent Titus from Alexandria to Jerusalem with "a select part of his army" (4.11.5). Tacitus himself records that the Gauls read the Capitol fire as a sign that Rome's rule was ending (4:54). No ancient source we opened links the two fires or says Romans saw the second as a reply to the first. This is a Claude idea, not a published argument.

spec.title: Claude's theory: one oracle, three readers
spec.body: Tacitus (5:13), Josephus (Jewish War 6.5.4) and Suetonius (Vespasian 4) all report an old saying that rulers coming from Judea would rule the world, and all three give it to Vespasian. None names a verse. Candidates in the Bible are Genesis 49:10, Numbers 24:17 and Daniel 7:13-14, which Christians read of Jesus. The Flavians used the saying, and Josephus's reading helped his own standing with them. Which verse lay behind it is a guess.
